newsitem.title: INDIA: India stock rally spurs renewed retail interest.
newsitem.headline: India stock rally spurs renewed retail interest.

text.p: A rally in Indian stocks, spurred by government policy promises, is slowly luring small investors back into the market, analysts said on Tuesday.
"We are seeing a return of confidence... Retail investors are slowly picking up stocks," said Ramdeo Agarwal, head of research at local brokerage Motilal Oswal.
"People are quite hopeful...there is renewed interest in the market."
Indian stocks have raced ahead this year, boosted by government promises of policy measures to bolster industrial growth and revive sluggish markets. No details have been announced.
At the close on Tuesday, the benchmark 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) index was up 34.28 points, or 0.99 percent, to a provisional 3,487.44, stretching the rally into its sixth day.

Analysts said repeated positive statements by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and government officials had fuelled speculative bidding in blue chips and made way for a gradual return of retail investors to mid-cap stocks.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram is expected to present the 1997/98 (April-March) budget to parliament in late February.
"The market has run up very fast... A correction is necessary to sustain the rally," Agarwal said.
"Now (is the time) for the government to follow up by announcing the (policy) measures... The market is moving ahead in anticipation of the announcements."
Traders hope the government will give tax relief to the cement, steel and consumer goods industries that have been hit by a slowdown in demand and a squeeze on margins.
Ashish Kacholia, head of research at Prime Broking, said the rally had brought about a perceptible change in investor sentiment, stoking an appetite for smaller stocks.
"Investors are cautious buyers...they are looking at good quality," he said.
Since hitting a three-year low on December 4, the Bombay index has risen 755 points, or nearly 28 percent.
"High net-worth retail investors are going in for defensive stocks -- in the health care and pharmaceutical sectors," said E.Y. Rangoonwala, director at 21st Century Management Services.
"Generally, small investors come late to buy and are among the early sellers... They are largely waiting for the bullish trend to get confirmed."
Oswal's Agarwal said investors were shying away from cyclical stocks. "It's the non-cyclicals, like pharmaceuticals, in which buying interest is seen."
More than 20 million retail investors trade on the country's 23 exchanges.
